My knowledge here is limited, but a hashcode can be used to verify authenticity/integrity, or for organization and sorting. To get a basic idea, let's say you have some ASCII text. 'A' = 65, 'B' = 66, etc... We could easily write a function that chews up some ASCII text and spits out an eight bit number. Just add all the numbers up, divide by 256 and take the remainder. This isn't a good hash function because it would be easy to come up with different text that evaluates to the same number, but it gives an idea of how it would work. With a longer hashcode you would be less likely to accidentally (or intentionally) produce altered text which produces the same hashcode as the original, and a more complex algorithm would make it harder for someone to produce a forgery (ex: malicious software masquerading as legitimate software) which is validated by the hash function.

First, I'm a professional software engineer and am reasonably versed in cryptology. Reasonably.

First, the basics. A hash is a one way method for disguising text. Not a perfect way of putting it, but you get the idea. There are three requirements for a mathematically sound hash. A given text must always hash to the same result. SteelKidney will always hash to faf25c72007c17c960286d78951af470 using MD5. Second, no two distinct text strings can generate the same hash. So no other string can hash to faf25c72007c17c960286d78951af470. Only SteelKidney. Finally, there must be no way of mathematically deriving the original source text from the hash. This is the big one. There's no decrypt key and there's no algorithm for getting the string faf25c72007c17c960286d78951af470 and getting SteelKidney from it. Even if you know it's MD5 and you know the math behind the MD5 algorithm it's still impossible. Actually, it isn't with MD5, which is why you shouldn't use MD5. But for purposes of an overview, those are the rules.

If all you want to do is understand the concept, this is all you need to know. It's not that complicated a concept. But if you want to implement it, you have a few more things to understand.

You "break" a hash by trial and error. Either by brute force, where you cycle through as many strings as you can, hash each one, and compare to the hash you want to reverse. Eventually, you'll get there, but the trick is reducing the amount of time "eventually" takes. Or, you can use what's known as a rainbow table to perform a dictionary attack. This is exactly what it sounds like. You take common terms from the dictionary and common variations and start by hashing those. Against large sets of passwords, like the LinkedIn data theft, you'll get a lot of hits this way. As an implementer, you need to understand this so you can defend against it. The methods fall roughly into three techniques.

First, select your hash algorithm well. MD5 and SHA1 are highly insecure because they're very fast. That means you can make, literally, millions of comparisons a second. An 8 character password will reasonably have 8^70 or so possible combinations, but if you're using a very fast algorithm you can rent some computing time and make all possible matches in about 2 seconds or so. Yeah. You read that right. Others, such as SHA512 and Blowfish, are much slower. Keep in mind, though, with today's computing speeds they aren't slow enough.

Which brings us to the second idea, salting. That means adding a meaningless set of data to the text to be hashed so that matching the text itself doesn't result in a correct match. As an example, you could salt SteelKidney to SteelKidney8cf68afb-2ff9-47fc-e37f-2d66a0840691. This does two things. First, it adds a string that's very difficult to predict, thus slowing down dictionary attacks. Second, it greatly lengthens the text, thus slowing down brute force attacks.

Sadly, this still isn't enough. So we do one more thing, a technique known as "stretching". That means continually hashing the results of the hash over many iterations. By many, I mean a thousand is a good starting point. This is really a time waster. Now we're getting to the point where SteelKidney8cf68afb-2ff9-47fc-e37f-2d66a0840691 isn't likely to be broken within any useful time period. And when computing power ramps up to where 1000 stretching iterations aren't enough, you can bump it to 2000. Or whatever.

Don't know exactly what you're looking for, but unless you really want to study the math behind it, that's about what you need to know on the subject.
